bugs: ShipOrderRequest::authorize() (app/Http/Requests/ShipOrderRequest.php:11) returns `$this->user()->is_staff` with a `bool` return type. If the user model was never loaded from the DB (for example a factory-made user passed to Sanctum::actingAs without is_staff set), the attribute is null, PHP throws a TypeError and the response is 500 instead of 403. I reproduced this with a probe. Real token-authenticated users come from the DB, so this mostly breaks tests, but it is brittle.

The mail is sent synchronously inside DB::afterCommit (app/Models/Order.php:58). If the mailer throws after the commit, the API returns 500 even though the order is already shipped. A retry then gets 409, so the customer is never emailed. There is no queue or retry path.
antipatterns: app/Http/Requests/ShipOrderRequest.php:11: the staff check sits inline in FormRequest::authorize. An OrderPolicy with the route's ->can('ship','order') would be more reusable.
app/Mail/OrderShipped.php:11: the mailable is not ShouldQueue, so SMTP latency and failures land in the request.

tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:128-131: the test calls DB::rollBack() manually inside a DB::transaction closure instead of throwing to simulate a back-office failure. This is a hacky rollback simulation.
app/Models/Order.php:47-48: the in-memory status is set and synced manually. It is fine, but after an outer rollback the instance still says Shipped.
strengths: Concurrency-safe claim: a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status != shipped plus a check on rows affected (Order.php:41-45). A stale-instance probe correctly got 409 with no duplicate points.
Points use increment() inside the transaction, so they roll back with the outer transaction. The mail is deferred with DB::afterCommit, and a savepoint-rollback probe sent nothing.

Because Mail::to()->send runs inside the afterCommit callback, Mail::fake respects rollback. The tests use idiomatic Mail::assertSent/assertNothingSent and assert nothing is sent before the outer commit.

The one comment says what breaks if someone changes the code. The Markdown mailable, enum cast, factory states and unique DB constraint are all in place, along with a test that the unique constraint is enforced.
Good test coverage: 401, 403 including the customer, 404, 422 datasets, 409 with no side effects, a repeat call, rounding dataset, rollback and commit paths, and mail content.

bugs: Testability gap in the focus area: MailFake ignores the mailable's ->afterCommit(). With Mail::fake(), a rolled-back ship() still shows OrderShipped as queued (my probe's assertNothingQueued failed). Any Mail::fake-based test of the rollback requirement gives a false failure, and a regression that drops afterCommit() would not be caught by fake-based tests (tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:49-57). Runtime behaviour on the sync and array transports is correct.
antipatterns: tests/Feature/ShipOrderTest.php:12-15,42-46: tests reach into Mail::mailer('array')->getSymfonyTransport()->messages() and Symfony message internals instead of Laravel's mail assertions. This is brittle and couples the tests to the transport config.
app/Models/Order.php:57: the comment just narrates framework behaviour.
app/Http/Controllers/ShipOrderController.php:13: double-quoted strings are inconsistent with the rest of the codebase.
app/Policies/OrderPolicy.php:9: has the same `bool` return of a possibly-null attribute, which only works because UserFactory hard-codes is_staff=false.
strengths: Authorization uses an OrderPolicy with ->can('ship','order') on the route, which is the idiomatic Laravel approach. The FormRequest only validates.
Same atomic conditional-UPDATE claim as impl-1. Enum values are bound directly in the query, and throw_if takes the exception class. The stale-instance probe returned 409.

The mailable is ShouldQueue with SerializesModels and ->afterCommit(), which is robust in production: no SMTP failure inside the request, and nothing is queued if the outer transaction rolls back. The savepoint-rollback probe passed.
The rollback test throws inside an outer transaction, which is realistic. It also covers the commit path, zero cents, adding to existing points, and a max-length validation case.
UserFactory sets explicit defaults for is_staff and points, and the shipment factory defaults to a shipped order, which is consistent.

v.rationale:
Both implementations claim the order the same way: a conditional UPDATE that is safe under concurrent requests, points incremented inside the transaction, a unique order_id, and a 409 thrown as a ConflictHttpException. In probes, both blocked a second ship from a stale model instance and sent no mail after a savepoint rollback. The ranking comes down to how each handles mail and how idiomatic the tests are.

Impl-1 defers a synchronous send with DB::afterCommit. That keeps Mail::fake accurate, so its tests use clean Laravel mail assertions, including an assertion that nothing is sent before the outer commit. Its weaknesses are a FormRequest authorize() that returns 500 when is_staff is null (test-only in practice) and synchronous mail after commit, with no retry if sending fails.

Impl-2 has the better production design: a policy with the route's can() middleware, and a queued mailable using ->afterCommit(). But MailFake ignores afterCommit, so the authors had to dig into the array transport's Symfony messages to test the rollback requirement. Its own Mail::fake test would not catch a regression that dropped afterCommit. That weakens the "testable mail" focus and makes the tests more brittle.

On balance, impl-1 does better on the task's stated focus and has cleaner tests, so it ranks first by a narrow margin.
